questions.prompt: A session has been open for three hours. You ask one more short question and the reported cost jumps. Why is the short question not cheap?
options: Short prompts are billed at a higher per-token rate to discourage them
The whole conversation is sent again on every request, so the short question carries the whole session with it
Three hours of wall-clock time accrues a background charge each time you send anything
The rate limit from Lesson 11 adds a surcharge per request
questions.explanation: There is no per-request premium and no time-based surcharge — the cost is a direct function of tokens sent, and every request re-sends the accumulated conversation plus files read plus tool output. Option C gestures at background requests, which exist but are tiny and would not explain a jump that scales with session length. Option D reaches forward to a lesson not yet taught and describes a limit, not a price.

questions.prompt: You must locate every caller of `parseConfig()`. Which ask is most likely to keep tokens down without losing the answer?
options: Find every place parseConfig is used and paste each match with 40 lines of surrounding context
Search the whole repo for parseConfig and explain each hit
List the file path and line number of every call site of parseConfig. Do not read surrounding code.
Understand how configuration parsing works in this codebase, including every usage of parseConfig
questions.explanation: Cost is driven by what comes back into context, and file reads plus surrounding context are permanent. Asking for path and line only returns the evidence you need. Option A looks narrower than B but the 40 lines of context multiply the read count. Option D is a comprehension task disguised as a locate task, which drags in far more files than the question requires.

questions.prompt: You estimate a file's cost at characters divided by four, then the real count comes back noticeably lower. What is the most likely reason?
options: The /4 rule only applies to prose, and code has a different average density
You counted the wrong file's characters
Common words are split into fewer tokens than the rule assumes, so the rule over-estimates
Some of the file was served from cache and not billed
questions.explanation: The /4 rule assumes roughly four characters per token. High-frequency English collapses into single tokens shorter than that average, which pushes the real count below the estimate. Option A is wrong because code is usually less compressible than prose, so it skews the other way. Option D is a real mechanism but it changes latency, not the token count you are comparing against.
